items.title: Researchers find training a single transformer layer can match or exceed full-parameter reinforcement learning gains across multiple models and tasks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Is One Layer Enough? A Single Transformer Layer Matches Full-Parameter RL Train
items.summary:
Researchers have discovered that training a single transformer layer can achieve reinforcement learning (RL) improvements comparable to or even exceeding those obtained by training all parameters in large language models. This finding challenges the common assumption that all layers contribute equally to RL gains and suggests that most benefits are concentrated in a small subset of layers, often in the middle of the transformer stack.

The study analyzed seven models across different families, RL algorithms, and tasks such as mathematical reasoning, code generation, and decision-making. The researchers introduced a metric called layer contribution to quantify how much each layer contributes to RL improvements, revealing a consistent pattern where middle layers have the highest impact while input and output layers contribute less. This pattern held across various datasets, tasks, and model architectures, indicating a stable structural characteristic of transformer models during RL training.

items.title: Senior SWE-Bench launches open-source benchmark evaluating AI agents on senior software engineer tasks with realistic instructions and runtime bug investigations [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Senior SWE-Bench: open-source benchmark that assesses agents as senior engineers
items.summary:
Senior SWE-Bench is an open-source benchmark designed to evaluate AI agents on tasks typical of senior software engineers, using realistic, naturally phrased instructions and complex runtime bug investigations. Unlike traditional benchmarks that treat agents like junior engineers with over-specified requirements, Senior SWE-Bench focuses on multi-phase, multi-stack feature development and debugging tasks sourced from real pull requests requiring significant runtime analysis.

The benchmark assesses agents not only on correctness but also on code quality and adherence to best practices, reflecting the nuanced decision-making expected of senior engineers. Current top-performing AI models still fail to achieve senior-level performance on over 75% of tasks, highlighting the challenge of replicating expert software engineering skills in AI agents.

items.title: Researchers say text AI watermarks will remain easy to remove despite EU AI Act requirements starting August 2026 [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Text AI watermarks will always be trivial to remove
items.summary:
The European Union AI Act, enforceable from August 2026, mandates that all AI-generated text must be detectable through watermarks. However, researchers highlight that watermarking text is inherently challenging due to the compressed nature of language, which limits subtle modifications without affecting quality. Current methods, such as Google's SynthID, embed detectable patterns in token selection, but these watermarks remain vulnerable to removal or disruption.

Text watermarking differs significantly from image watermarking because even minor changes in text are noticeable, making it difficult to conceal signatures without degrading output quality. While some AI providers use probabilistic token sampling to embed watermarks, these techniques require careful balancing to maintain text coherence and are computationally intensive to verify. The EU's requirement for free watermarking services adds further complexity for AI developers.

Despite these efforts, the effectiveness of text watermarks is limited, as they can be removed or altered, raising questions about the reliability of watermarking as a sole method for AI content detection. This ongoing challenge suggests that AI labs will need to explore multiple strategies to comply with regulations while preserving model performance and user experience.

items.originalTitle: Bank of England explores trading 'kill switches' to contain AI meltdowns
items.summary:
The Bank of England is considering implementing kill switches in trading systems to prevent market disruptions caused by autonomous artificial intelligence (AI) agents. This initiative responds to concerns that current regulatory frameworks may not adequately address the risks posed by AI-driven trading, which can operate at high speed and scale without consistent human oversight. The move aims to enhance financial market stability by enabling rapid intervention if AI models behave unpredictably or cause volatility.

Deputy Governor Sarah Breeden highlighted that AI systems are increasingly capable of autonomously executing complex trading strategies, raising the possibility of amplified market stress if multiple AI agents react similarly to triggers. The Bank is collaborating with international partners to simulate AI behaviors and explore governance measures, including circuit breakers or kill switches, to contain potential AI-induced market meltdowns. Additionally, there are growing concerns about AI's role in cyber vulnerabilities, prompting calls for faster patching and stronger cooperation among financial institutions to maintain cyber resilience.

This change marks a reversal from earlier approaches where longer prompts with many examples were necessary to guide AI behavior. As the models have evolved, they now require shorter prompts that allow for more imaginative responses, indicating a new phase in AI prompt design focused on context rather than explicit instructions.

items.originalTitle: Launching chokepoints – mapping the bottlenecks in the AI infrastructure stack
items.summary:
Chokepoints.ai has created an interactive map detailing the AI compute supply chain for 2026, identifying 580 market nodes and 562 dependencies across ten infrastructure layers. The analysis highlights 95 chokepoints—markets dominated by a few players that control terms downstream—and 130 bottlenecks under strain, spanning from raw materials to applications. Key chokepoints include semiconductor manufacturing dominated by TSMC and ASML, compute hardware led by NVIDIA, and power generation constrained by a three-OEM oligopoly.

The map reveals significant concentration in critical areas such as rare-earth refining in China, EUV lithography, and liquid cooling for data centers. While cloud infrastructure remains competitive, supply constraints in physical components and permitting limit expansion. The report also notes that capital availability is not the bottleneck; rather, execution capacity, skilled labor, and regulatory permitting are the main constraints affecting the AI compute build-out.

This comprehensive overview underscores the complex dependencies and vulnerabilities in the AI supply chain, raising questions about how these chokepoints and bottlenecks will impact the pace and scale of AI infrastructure development in the near future.

Users can download their data before the app is removed, and all personal data will be deleted after shutdown.

Impeccable allows users to give nuanced commands like making a section "bolder" or "quieter," translating design vocabulary into actionable instructions for AI.

Bakaus highlights the importance of embedding professional design concepts into AI skills to avoid generic or uniform results and to better express expert intent. He also notes the evolving roles of designers and engineers as their disciplines converge, urging professionals to move beyond routine tasks toward higher-level creative and strategic thinking. His approach aims to balance AI capabilities with human expertise to improve design processes without replacing human creativity.

items.originalSummary:
Financial data companies such as FactSet and Moody’s appear to have made progress reassuring investors that they won’t be replaced by finance-focused AI tools. But investors may have new questions these days around how the uncertainty of AI costs will affect usage of these businesses’ products.

Investors were spooked when Anthropic and others touted AI products for finance and other professions earlier this year. Companies like FactSet, Moody’s, S&P Global and LSEG, which all make money in part by selling information like market data, company financials and risk analytics, were hit by a market selloff.

Stocks have recovered at least partly since then, and the firms made a pretty compelling argument that rising usage of AI tools doesn’t hurt the value of their data. Banks, asset managers and other regulated customers still need licensed, current information that they can easily verify and audit. 

These firms have also added AI features to their products and made data available in formats customers can access through their own AI tools. Overall, they say AI adoption is positive for demand, because an AI agent can consume far more data than any human analyst. 

But things aren’t proving quite that simple. In recent months, businesses have become more focused on the rising cost of AI usage and many companies are adopting measures to keep AI spending under control. That’s raising a fresh set of AI-related questions for data sellers. 

A big question is who pays the cost of the tokens needed to run AI-powered data analysis. The answer depends on how the access to the data is structured, and whether a customer is using the data through their own AI tools or not. How much more customers are willing to pay for AI to run data analysis is another question. And like AI costs themselves, data consumption by AI tools can be unpredictable, because an agent might rerun queries or try lots of data sets. The overall picture might be unnerving for investors in a business where they’ve long prized relatively steady revenue streams. 

On Wednesday, FactSet CFO Joshua Warren said AI tokens “were not a line item that we really thought about in 2025.” Those costs are showing up in FactSet’s own spending as it uses AI internally and builds AI-powered products for customers. FactSet says it has internal controls like budgeting and model routing, and a recently expanded Google partnership gave it preferential token pricing.

When it comes to customer demand, FactSet executives noted that AI products were proving to be a source of growth and commanding richer contracts, but they also said customers are still not clear on what their own consumption will be, so want flexibility in pricing. 

“In an AI world, right now, there is a lot of value that clients are placing on that,” FactSet CEO Sanoke Viswanathan said, and the company is adding provisions for “new consumption patterns” as customers experiment.

Moody’s, for its part, appeared to be getting ahead of both sides of the cost question. In a June investor Q&A with a JPMorgan research analyst, a Moody’s executive noted that customers bear the AI token costs when they use its data through tools like Claude Enterprise, ChatGPT or Microsoft Copilot. They added that Moody’s can help customers keep a lid on those costs, including by packaging its data with instructions that help AI agents use it quickly and efficiently. Moody’s also builds token costs into contracts with customers that are using its own AI tools, but it says it closely monitors those costs through routing and other measures.

To be sure, there isn’t much evidence yet that AI has moved the needle either way. Financial data businesses aren’t exactly blockbuster growth stories, but their recent growth rates still look broadly similar to before the AI scare. 

If anything, the most noticeable impact from the AI boom might be outside these companies’ data subscriptions. LSEG, which also owns the London Stock Exchange and other markets businesses, has suggested that AI is accelerating decision making and activity in general, which translates into more trading activity and risk management needs. Markets revenue jumped in the first quarter, helped by strong trading volumes. 

Meanwhile Moody’s and S&P Global have both said that a surge in debt issuance tied to AI infrastructure spending has boosted their credit ratings businesses, which make money in part when companies issue new debt and pay to have it rated.

The next question is how far into finance these companies can reach with their AI businesses. FactSet executives said on Wednesday that the wealth management industry is still in the early stages of AI adoption, but financial advisers present a big potential customer pool. That could also turn into client-facing tools for people using wealth and consumer financial services. 

New types of users could well have a very different take on AI costs and payoffs than the big existing financial customers, which could introduce further complications around fees and pricing. Meanwhile, the rest of the financial data crowd are due to report results in the coming weeks. We’ll see how the narrative continues to change.

items.originalTitle: LLMs are stuck in a groupthink groove. This startup is trying to get them out.
items.summary:
Australian startup Springboards has developed a new large language model (LLM) called Flint, designed to produce more diverse and creative responses than mainstream models like ChatGPT and Claude. Flint aims to address the common issue of groupthink in current LLMs, which often generate predictable and similar answers to open-ended questions. The startup embraces a degree of hallucination in responses to enhance variety and creativity, which could benefit brainstorming and planning tasks.

Springboards' Flint model was demonstrated by generating varied answers to prompts where other models typically repeated the same responses, such as random numbers or campaign taglines. Research has shown that many LLMs converge on similar outputs due to training on comparable data and tasks, limiting their originality. Springboards offers Flint as an alternative for creative professionals seeking a broader range of ideas, integrating it into a tool that combines outputs from multiple models for enhanced brainstorming.

items.originalTitle: Cloudflare’s new policy pushes AI companies to pay for publishers’ content
items.summary:
Cloudflare has announced a new policy requiring AI companies to separate their web crawlers used for traditional search from those used for AI training and agents by September 15, 2026. If companies fail to comply, their mixed-use crawlers will be blocked by default on many ad-hosting publisher sites. This change aims to protect publishers' content and intellectual property while maintaining discoverability through search and AI services.

The policy will affect new and existing Cloudflare customers, particularly those using free plans, and reflects a broader effort to create a sustainable ecosystem amid increasing non-human internet traffic. Cloudflare is also collaborating with partners like Ceramic.ai and You.com to enable publishers to monetize their content when accessed by AI services, evolving its Pay Per Crawl model into a Pay Per Use system that charges AI companies based on the value generated from the content rather than just data fetching.

Software developers are starting to combine the two most successful uses of large language models: coding and customer support.

Specifically, they’re using AI to automate the process of turning customer complaints about software issues or feature requests into new code. Previously, that could be a long and tedious process, which involved sending customer support tickets to a company’s support team, directing those issues to the relevant engineer, and coding up and testing a fix to the issue. 

AI cybersecurity startup Semgrep, for instance, routes customer complaints about bugs in its app or requests for new features to Anthropic’s Claude model, founder and CEO Isaac Evans said. Claude handles the fix or codes the new features in a sandboxed, isolated version of Semgrep’s app. After a human engineer tests the changes, Semgrep merges them into the real Semgrep app, which primarily helps developers scan their code for bugs and vulnerabilities, he said. Right now, Semgrep is using this approach for a handful of customer support tickets per month, but Evans expects that number to grow quickly, he said.

items.originalTitle: You Can Now Sound the Alarm on AI Behaving Badly
items.summary:
Researchers have launched FLARE-AI, a crowdsourced website designed to report and track safety issues in AI systems, such as malware generation, data leaks, and harmful behaviors. The platform allows users to submit reports that can be verified and routed to AI developers and organizations like MITRE, aiming to create a centralized system for identifying AI flaws.

Developed by a collaboration of 49 AI experts from 32 organizations, FLARE-AI addresses the current lack of a unified reporting mechanism for AI problems, which range from cybersecurity risks to psychological harm and bias. The initiative supports transparency and accountability in AI development, complementing recent legislative efforts in the US to establish standards and centralized databases for AI flaw reporting.

As AI systems become more powerful and autonomous, FLARE-AI could play a crucial role in managing emerging risks and encouraging safer AI deployment. The platform also faces challenges such as handling large volumes of reports and ensuring credibility, but it represents a significant step toward coordinated oversight of AI safety concerns.

items.title: Commerce Department lifts export controls on Anthropic’s Fable 5 and Mythos 5 AI models after company adds new security guardrails to restrict sensitive queries [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Anthropic Added a New Security Measure to Get Back Into the Trump Administration’s Good Graces
items.summary:
The U.S. Commerce Department has lifted export controls on Anthropic's Fable 5 and Mythos 5 AI models after the company implemented new security measures to restrict access to sensitive queries. These measures include extending existing safeguards that redirect certain user requests to a less advanced AI model, Opus 4.8, to prevent exploitation of restricted capabilities related to cybersecurity and biology.

This decision followed concerns raised by the administration about users circumventing restrictions by rephrasing queries, which led to the temporary removal of Fable 5 from export. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick confirmed that Anthropic agreed to proactively detect and address security risks posed by the models, and the department's Center for AI Standards and Innovation deemed the safeguards sufficiently robust. However, some challenges remain, as the Department of Defense has yet to lift a supply chain risk designation against the company.
